summary: Instructions from Bob Braden for connecting to IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) at UCLA's Campus Computing Network over the ARPANET. A user opens a standard Telnet connection to socket 1 and enters a TSO command. The note lists the possible replies, such as a welcome message or a notice that TSO is unavailable, and what to do next.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 377 explains how to reach UCLA-CCN's IBM Time Sharing Option (TSO) through Telnet. It tells users how to start a session, handle line input and interrupts, and work around a known problem.

questions: how to use tso over the arpanet
subtitle: Instructions for connecting to UCLA-CCN's IBM Time Sharing Option over Telnet.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed instructions for reaching IBM's Time Sharing Option service at UCLA-CCN from a remote terminal.
tldr.mechanism: The user opens a Telnet connection to socket 1, enters TSO, and follows the response. The server handles line editing and translates input for TSO.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents the service's responses, input conventions, interrupt behavior, timeouts, and a workaround for an interrupt bug.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 377's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It documents how to use the UCLA-CCN TSO service in August 1972.

sections.title: Opening a TSO Session
sections.content:
UCLA-CCN makes IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) available on socket 1 using standard Telnet. A remote user performs the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) to that socket and sends TSO CR LF.

A welcome message followed by ! means TSO is available, and the user should enter a TSO LOGON command. If TSO is unavailable, the user should check its schedule and contact the CCN help service if appropriate. If all TSO ports are busy, the user should try again later and report frequent recurrence to the Technical Liaison.
sections.plainLanguage: Connect to socket 1 and enter TSO followed by the line ending. The response tells you whether to log in, check the schedule, or try again later.

sections.title: Entering Lines and Interrupting Output
sections.content:
TSO processes input one line at a time. It scans input after an end-of-line or an INS interrupt, and sends ! when it is waiting for input. The line ending is CR LF; local echoing at the user's site is required.

A user can interrupt TSO output with an INS and DATA MARK pair, using Telnet value X'80'. A TIP user can use SEND SYNC. The CCN server Telnet provides line editing: control-X deletes the current line, control-H deletes the previous character, and control-I inserts a space. The note lists disconnect timeouts of 5 minutes for incomplete output, 2 minutes for an unmatched interrupt pair, and 20 minutes while TSO waits for input.
sections.plainLanguage: TSO reads a complete line at a time and shows ! when it is ready for input. The guide lists keys for editing and a special signal for stopping output.

sections.title: A Workaround for an Interrupt Bug
sections.content:
The memo describes a case where a program is waiting for terminal input and the user wants to suspend it without supplying that input. An INS/DATA MARK pair is supposed to transfer control to a higher level, but a bug in the network interface to TSO causes the interrupt to be ignored in this case.

The suggested workaround is to define a software break string with TERM INPUT (!!!!), without quotation marks. An input line containing four consecutive exclamation points then acts as an interrupt. If other characters come before the four marks, they act as a line delete instead.
sections.plainLanguage: One interrupt does not work while a program is waiting for input. The guide says to define four exclamation points as a substitute break string.

sections.title: Character Translation and Editing
sections.content:
The server Telnet accepts upper- and lowercase input, translates lowercase to uppercase, and normally returns uppercase output. It performs line editing before passing input to TSO. Control-X deletes the current line, control-H deletes the previous character, and control-I inserts one space; other ASCII control characters are removed before editing.

Input is translated to EBCDIC using the rules for a NETRJS remote operator console in RFC 189. The memo gives mappings for some characters not shared by ASCII and EBCDIC, says six ASCII graphics without EBCDIC counterparts become question marks, and states that all Telnet controls except DATA MARK are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The server changes input to the character format TSO expects and handles several editing keys. The guide also lists how it treats characters and Telnet controls that TSO does not use.

references.text: Braden, R. T., "Interim NETRJS Specifications", RFC 189, July 1971.
